analysis.one_liner: Exempts shipping to Alaska, Hawaii, and U.S. territories from Jones Act requirements.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Jones Act, a ship moving goods between U.S. ports must be built in the United States, mostly American-owned, and mostly American-crewed. Because few ships meet those tests, shipping between the mainland and Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico, and the territories is expensive and dominated by a handful of carriers. This bill would lift those requirements on those routes, but only if the route already has at least three independent shipping companies competing on it, each carrying at least 20% of the cargo, so competition—not a blanket repeal—does the work of lowering prices.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents and businesses in Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, Guam, and other U.S. territories, who pay some of the highest shipping and consumer goods costs in the country. Importers, farmers, retailers, and manufacturers shipping goods on those routes would also pay less, and consumers would see savings passed through to shelf prices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents of Hawaii, Alaska, and U.S. territories

how_it_helps.text: The bill removes the Jones Act requirements—that vessels be U.S.-built, at least 75% U.S.-owned, and mostly U.S.-crewed—for shipping on routes to and from Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico, and the insular territories, where those requirements apply to nearly all cargo traffic.

The exemption is conditioned, not automatic: it applies only where at least three independent owners or operators of coastwise-qualified vessels regularly serve the route and each carries at least 20% of the cargo volume, so a competing market must actually exist before foreign or cheaper carriers are allowed in.
Supporters introduced it to add competition on noncontiguous trade routes, where the existing coastwise laws leave little or no competition and shipping costs are correspondingly high.

analysis.who_pays: U.S.-flagged Jones Act carriers that currently serve these routes with little competition, which would face new rivals with lower costs. U.S. shipyards that build and maintain the small domestic Jones Act fleet would lose protected work, and U.S. merchant mariner jobs on those routes would be at risk from lower-wage foreign crews.
analysis.who_pays_short: Jones Act carriers, U.S. shipyards, and mariners

drawbacks.text: The Jones Act's defenders argue that the requirements sustain a U.S. shipbuilding industrial base and a pool of American crews that the military relies on for sealift in emergencies; opening noncontiguous routes to foreign-built, foreign-crewed ships would shrink that base.

Jobs for American merchant mariners on routes to Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and the territories would be exposed to competition from foreign crews working under other countries' wage and labor rules.

The trigger conditions are demanding: a route must already have three independent operators each carrying at least 20% of the volume, which on most routes would not be met, so in practice the bill may change little even if enacted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit is real but uneven: it would lower shipping costs for people in places that pay the country's highest freight costs, while the cost falls on a small, protected domestic shipping and shipbuilding sector and its workforce. The strongest honest criticism is national security—the U.S.-built, U.S.-crewed fleet exists partly for military readiness—and the trigger design, which limits the bill's actual reach. On balance the bill's direct aim was to reduce a cost of living that falls hardest on ordinary households in Hawaii, Puerto Rico, Alaska, and the territories.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation Subcommittee in April 2023, and the committee never took it up; it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ed Case (D-HI) introduced the bill on April 13, 2023, joined by Rep. James Moylan (R-GU), the bill's sole cosponsor.

The House referred the bill to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee the day it was introduced, and on April 14, 2023 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation.
No further action was ever recorded—no hearing, markup, or vote—and the bill died at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Jones Act carriers that dominate shipping to Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and the territories, along with the U.S. shipyards that build and service their vessels, are better off: the coastwise law that protects their markets from foreign competition remains intact because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Rep. James Moylan
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as the sole original cosponsor.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after subcommittee referral; never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote in the nearly two years remaining in the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship—a Hawaii Democrat and a Guam Republican—but only one cosponsor total, and no vote was ever taken, so no party split on it was ever recorded.

industries.note: A small group of carriers dominates shipping between the mainland and Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and the territories under the Jones Act, charging some of the highest freight rates in the country. The bill would have exposed them to competition on those routes, so their interest ran against lower consumer prices. They benefit from the outcome because the law stayed intact.

Jones Act rules guarantee shipyards a captive market of domestic-built vessels. Opening noncontiguous routes to foreign-built ships would have reduced that protected work, though the bill's narrow trigger would have limited the effect.

industries.industry: U.S. merchant mariners and maritime unions
industries.note: American crews would have faced competition from foreign crews on noncontiguous routes. Their interest in preserving Jones Act crewing rules ran against lower shipping costs for consumers in those places.
Where the exemption's competition trigger is met, foreign carriers could carry cargo on routes currently closed to them, giving shippers and residents cheaper options.
